# Sharing workflows across a teaching team

Once a workflow works for one module, write it down as a file the agent can follow, and share the file. A department then needs each workflow to be worked out only once for all its lecturers.

**What is worth sharing.**

| Item | What it is | Who benefits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Module template | The empty folder layout and a skeleton instruction file (chapter 3) | Anyone starting or inheriting a module |
| Workflow files | Step-by-step instructions for a recurring task: new lecture, new problem set, annual update, stress test | Colleagues doing the same task |
| Checker | The independent checker from chapter 8, as a stored definition | Lecturers and teaching assistants |
| Statement template | The student-facing AI statement (chapter 10) | The whole programme |

**How to write a workflow file.** Write it as you would brief a capable teaching assistant who has never seen the module:

- What the task is and when to use it.
- What inputs it needs and where they are.
- The steps, in order, including the checks from chapter 8.
- What the finished output looks like and where it goes.
- What the agent must not do.

Test it by running it on a module other than the one it was written for. If it only works on your module, the module-specific parts belong in the instruction file.

**Building a written standard for the reviewer.** The third review pass in chapter 8 needs a document that says how your material should be written. It is built from your own work.

1. **Collect examples.** Five to ten pieces you consider your best: lecture notes, slides, problem sets, or papers if the standard is for research writing.
2. **Have the agent extract the rules.** Ask it to read them and list what is consistent: sentence and paragraph length, how a slide is structured, how a result is introduced, how equations are referenced, what is never done.
3. **Edit the rules yourself.** Delete what is accidental, correct what it misread, and add the rules you know you follow that the examples did not show.
4. **Add pairs of examples.** For each important rule, one passage that breaks it and the corrected version. The pair gives the reviewer something concrete to match.
5. **Add a list of what to flag.** The phrases and constructions you do not want, including those typical of machine-written text.
6. **Say how to report.** Findings as a list with location, the rule broken and a suggested fix. No rewriting.
7. **Test it on old material.** Run the reviewer on something you wrote before the standard existed, and on something an agent wrote. Adjust rules that produce false alarms.
8. **Keep it current.** Each time you correct the agent's writing by hand, ask whether the correction is a rule. If so, add it.

One to three pages is enough. A standard built this way is specific to its author, so share the method and the template with colleagues rather than your own rules. A skeleton is in the appendix.

**Where to keep shared files.** Keep them in a departmental repository or shared drive, with one owner per file, and keep that location free of student data and of assessment content: workflows and templates only.

**Teaching assistants.** Give assistants the checker and the problem-set workflow but not the assessment folder. Agree in advance what they may use an agent for, and apply the same rule to all assistants on a module.

**Handing a module over.** The instruction file with its decisions log, the figure and solution scripts, and the workflow files together are the handover. A successor can ask the agent to explain how any week's material was built and regenerate it.

> **In Claude Code.** A workflow file is a [skill](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills): a folder containing a `SKILL.md`, stored in `.claude/skills/<name>/` inside the module folder, or in `~/.claude/skills/<name>/` for personal use across modules. It runs when you type `/<name>`, or automatically when its description matches the task. Sharing is by committing `.claude/skills/` to the shared repository.
>
> The checker is a subagent definition in `.claude/agents/`. Skills follow the open Agent Skills standard, so the same files are usable in other tools that support it.
